name: Deera Square
label: Deera Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Deera Square' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Deera Square'.
notes: Historic public square beside the Grand Mosque.

text.description: Deera Square is a large open public square in the old heart of Riyadh. It is also called Justice Square or Safa Square, and its Arabic name is Sāḥat ad-Dayrah. It photographs well because the wide paved space gives you room to step back. The fountains sit in the foreground, and the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque fills the background. The square sits next to the al-Hukm Palace compound in the Qasr al-Hukm District. In the past it was the place where public executions were carried out, but it had stopped hosting them by 2019. Keep that in mind: take calm, respectful photos of the open space and the mosque, and keep the government and palace buildings out of your shots, as they should not be photographed. For a second picture, the mud-brick walls and watchtowers of Al Masmak Fort, at the edge of the square, make a good contrast between old and modern Riyadh. Early evening light, around golden hour, is the time to aim for, when the mosque and paving glow warmly. Move into the open expanse and face the mosque. Include some of the fountains and paving for depth, and wait a moment for people to move through the frame. Check opening hours before you plan a visit to the fort.
text.geographic_location: Deera Square is in the Ad-Dirah neighbourhood of central Riyadh, in the Qasr al-Hukm District. It sits next to the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque and the al-Hukm Palace compound.
text.directions_text: Head for the Ad-Dirah and Qasr al-Hukm area of Riyadh and look for the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque beside the square. The phone icon on the map is about 240 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the paved expanse, the fountains and the mosque together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the fountains in front. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the mosque.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 240 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there the photo shows the open paved expanse with its fountains, and the mosque filling the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the mosque on the upper third line, with the fountains and paving in the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the mosque's vertical lines stay straight. For a different picture, Al Masmak Fort at the square's edge gives you old mud-brick walls and watchtowers beside the modern square. Keep the palace and government buildings out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the building does not wash out. Live Photos can catch the movement of the fountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, when the light is warm and softer on the mosque.

text.access_note: Deera Square is an open public space, but check the official site before you go, especially for Al Masmak Fort, which is closed on Fridays and may have changed hours.

name: Kingdom Centre
label: Kingdom Centre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kingdom Centre' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/264745917: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Kingdom Centre' (440 m across).
notes: Skyscraper with the huge open arch and sky bridge.

text.description:
Kingdom Centre is a 99-storey tower, about 302 m tall, finished in 2002 and still one of the most recognisable shapes on the Riyadh skyline. Its almond-shaped body is topped by a huge inverted arch, which is nicknamed the "bottle opener". A glass-sided skybridge spans the opening. The lower floors hold offices, a hotel, apartments and the Al-Mamlaka shopping mall.

This spot is the Sky Bridge itself, high up between the two upper ends of the tower. From here you get a wide view over the city, with the suspended glass walkway as part of the scene. It works best around dusk, when the sky changes colour and the city lights start to come on. Visitors say phone photos come out well, though the glass can throw reflections back at you.

The bridge is a public observation deck reached by lift after paying admission, so check the official site before you go for current prices, hours and rules. If you would rather stay at street level, the tower also looks good from King Fahd Road, where you can fit in the whole curved top and the arch. Olaya Street gives a quieter frame with the tower rising above buildings and palms.

Take a few frames at different zoom levels, and wipe your phone lens before you start, as glass and lifts leave smudges.
text.geographic_location: Kingdom Centre stands in the al-Olaya district of central Riyadh. The complex includes the Al-Mamlaka shopping mall in the podium and the Four Seasons Hotel Riyadh in the tower.
text.directions_text: Head for the al-Olaya district and ask for Kingdom Centre or the Al-Mamlaka mall. Ask to be dropped at Kingdom Centre / Al-Mamlaka mall, then follow the signs for the Sky Bridge. The Sky Bridge is reached by lift from inside the building, so follow the signs for the observation deck. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the skyline and the glass bridge together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the broadest view, or a panorama along the windows. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single towers and streets far below.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Try to stand at a window with a clear view rather than a crowded gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level, with the city filling the lower two-thirds and the sky above. Press the phone lens gently against the glass, or close to it, so reflections drop away. Shade it with your hand or jacket if the glass still shows reflections. For a different picture, King Fahd Road shows the full tower and arch from outside, ideally against the sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the city and drag the exposure slider down a little so the sunset colours stay rich. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on the rail or window frame, because the exposure is longer. Live Photos can help you catch a moment when people walk through your frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just before sunset, so you catch the colour change over the city and the first lights coming on.

text.access_note: The Sky Bridge is a ticketed observation deck, and prices and opening hours vary, so check the official site before you go; the ground-level spots around the tower are outside the building.

name: Al Faisaliah Tower
label: Al Faisaliah Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'King Fahad Road' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'King Fahad Library Park' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1445986915: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Al Faisaliyah Tower' (76 m across).
notes: Golden glass-sphere topped tower on Olaya Street.

text.description:
Al Faisaliah Tower is one of the best-known landmarks in Riyadh, and its shape makes it easy to pick out. A tall, slim shaft rises to a golden sphere near the top, which is why the tower is also called the Star Dome. It stands 267 metres high in the Al-Olaya district and was designed by Foster + Partners. It was completed in 2000 and was the first skyscraper built in Saudi Arabia. For two years it was also the tallest building in the country. It is named after King Faisal bin Abdulaziz.

From the road, the tower's clean vertical lines and the sphere against the sky make a simple, strong photo. King Fahad Road is the main road past the tower, so you can stand back at road level and fit the whole height in. After dark the sphere is lit and stands out sharply against the night sky. For a different view, Olaya Street gives a second angle, with the golden globe at the top in low late-afternoon sun and the tower's full height in frame.

The tower is surrounded by other buildings and traffic, so take a few test shots and move along the road until the sphere sits clear of lamp posts and signs. Building work nearby has blocked the best angle at times, so be ready to adjust your position.
text.geographic_location: Al Faisaliah Tower is in the Al-Olaya district of central Riyadh, at the centre of the Al-Faisaliah Center complex.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed close to this spot, so head for the Al-Olaya district and make your way to King Fahad Road. Keep to the pavement and stay well back from the traffic when you stop to take photos. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole tower and some sky around it. If the sphere looks small, move to telephoto (2x-3x) to bring the top closer without walking into the traffic. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close, and keep the tower in the middle of the frame, because it will lean and stretch at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on King Fahad Road. The tower's exterior from the road, with the illuminated sphere standing out against the sky after dark. Stay on the pavement and well away from traffic. Because the tower is to the north-west, turn that way and frame the shaft upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it stands straight. Keep your phone level and leave a little space above the sphere so the top is not cut off. Vary the shot by waiting for a clear gap in the traffic or by trying a portrait-format frame to emphasise height. For a different angle, try Olaya Street, where the golden globe catches the late-afternoon sun.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: After dark, tap on the lit sphere to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so it keeps its detail and does not turn into a white blob. Use night mode and hold the phone against a wall, railing or your body to stay steady. Live Photos can catch moving headlights if you want some movement in the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset and after dark, when the sphere is lit. Sunset is around 5:15 pm in winter and 6:30 pm in summer, so arrive about 20 minutes early to try different angles in the fading light.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside of the tower from the public road, but going up inside, such as to the observation deck or restaurant, may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go; photography for personal use is generally fine, but professional shoots may need a permit.

name: National Museum of Saudi Arabia
label: National Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/40589074: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (369 m across).
notes: Museum of Arabian history in the King Abdulaziz Historical Center.

text.description: The National Museum of Saudi Arabia is the national museum of Saudi Arabia, covering the history of the Arabian Peninsula and the Saudi states, and the building is a good subject in its own right. It opened in 1999 as part of the King Abdulaziz Historical Centre. The architect, Raymond Moriyama, took his inspiration from the shapes and colours of the Red Sands dunes just outside Riyadh. The west facade, facing Murabba' Square, follows the soft line of a dune, and the whole layout forms a crescent pointing towards Mecca. That gentle curve and the warm sandy tones are what make it work in a phone photo: there are few hard edges, so the shapes read clearly even at a glance. The museum is very large, about 369 m across, so you will need to move around to see it properly. Al-Wadi Park lies to the north and al-Madi Park to the east, which gives you greenery and open space for stepping back. Inside, eight galleries run from the geology of Arabia through the early kingdoms and the Prophet's mission to the Saudi states and the Unification. Before shooting inside, check what is allowed. Outside, start with one wide shot of the curve, then move in for details such as the wall texture, the lines of the facade and people walking past, which give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: The museum is in the al-Murabba neighbourhood of Riyadh, beside Murabba' Square. It has al-Wadi Park to the north and al-Madi Park to the east.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so make your way to the al-Murabba area of Riyadh, for example by taxi. Ask to be dropped at the National Museum, on the Murabba' Square side if you can. From there, walk round the building to find the curved west facade. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the long curve of the facade, and the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of one section. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for details of the wall and entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Walk out to the Murabba' Square side, where the west facade is, and step back until the curve fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the horizon level, because the building's lines will look odd if the phone is tilted. Include a bit of the open square or the sky to show the dune-like shape. Take one wide shot, then a closer one of a single section with a person walking past for scale. The parks to the north and east give greener backdrops if you want a softer, more relaxed picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the sandy colour stays rich. For the full length of the building, try panorama mode and move the phone slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon usually suits the west facade best, as the low sun warms the sandy tones. Early morning is a calmer time with fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: Access to the grounds and the museum, and any rules on taking photos inside, may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Masmak Fortress
label: Masmak Fortress
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Al Thumairi Street' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Al Farzdaq Street' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1385940120: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Al Masmak Palace' (104 m across).
notes: Clay-brick fort in old Riyadh, scene of the 1902 recapture of the city.

text.description: Masmak Fortress is a clay and mudbrick fort in the old heart of Riyadh. It was begun in 1865 and finished in 1895, and in January 1902 it was the scene of the Battle of Riyadh, an important moment on the road to the unification of Saudi Arabia. It became a museum in 1995. It photographs well because the shape is so clear: thick sand-coloured walls, a heavy palm-wood gate, and a conical watchtower at each corner, each about 18 metres high. From across the road you can fit the whole front into one frame, rather than a cropped corner. The best place to do that is Al Thumairi Street, opposite the main facade, where the gate and all four towers sit together against the sky. The fort was restored and, according to one guide, reopened in mid-2025, so the walls may look different from older photos you have seen. For a second option, Deera Square gives you the fort across an open paved square, with modern buildings and street life in the foreground. Guides disagree on exactly where the square sits compared with the fort, so check the map. Stay on the pavement, watch for traffic, and leave a little space around the towers so they are not clipped at the top.
text.geographic_location: Masmak Fortress is in the ad-Dirah neighbourhood, in the old centre of Riyadh. It stands close to al-Hukm Palace in the Qasr al-Hukm District.
text.directions_text: Take a taxi or ride-hail to Masmak Fortress in the ad-Dirah area of old Riyadh. Ask to be dropped on Al Thumairi Street, then cross to the side opposite the fort's main facade. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road, which gives a natural view of the gate and towers. If traffic or the kerb limits how far you can step back, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to keep all four towers in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for close shots of a single tower or the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Al Thumairi Street (across the street from the fort's main facade). The full front of the fort with its gate and all four corner watchtowers, framed from the opposite side of the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the gate with the centre of the frame, so the walls stay straight and the two outer towers sit evenly at each side. Hold the phone level, as tilting it upwards will make the towers lean. For a different view, try Deera Square, which shows the facade across open paving with city life in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clay wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the walls keep their texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when guides say the clay walls take warm light well.

text.access_note: Photographing the outside from the street is free, but the fort is a museum, so check the official site before you go for visiting days, as one guide says it is closed on Fridays.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide (0.5x) may be needed to fit the whole facade if you cannot step back far enough from the pavement.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall towers appear to lean.
Traffic on Al Thumairi Street may limit where you can safely stand.
The map's stand-here point is about 2.3 km from the fort and does not match the Al Thumairi Street viewpoint opposite the facade; the placement should be verified on the map.

name: Murabba Palace
label: Murabba Palace
camera_source: Commons cluster (1 photos), weak. Moved 30 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 40 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/239102: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Murraba Palace' (65 m across).
notes: Historic palace of King Abdulaziz with mud-brick walls.

text.description:
Murabba Palace, whose Arabic name means 'the Square Palace', is a historic royal residence in Riyadh's al-Murabba neighbourhood and part of the King Abdulaziz Historical Center. King Abdulaziz ibn Saud had it built outside the walls of the old city. Work began in 1936, and he used it as his main home and official workplace from 1938 until his death in 1953. It is named after the 400 by 400 metre square it stands in. It has been a museum open to the public since 1999.

It photographs well because of its plain, solid, cube-like shape. It is a good example of traditional Najdi building: straw-reinforced adobe walls with engraved decoration, courtyards, and a large brick wall around the whole palace with nine gates. The materials are brick, local stone, tamarisk trunks and palm-leaf stalks. That gives you warm earthy colours and simple lines that look good on a phone screen.

For photos, use the wall and gate lines to lead the eye towards the palace. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines, because the building's strong vertical and horizontal edges look untidy if tilted. Then move in for close shots of the brick and plaster texture. Inside, the upper floor holds salons and exhibits of historic garments and crafts, so check the official site before you go to find out what you can see and photograph.
text.geographic_location: Murabba Palace is in the al-Murabba neighbourhood of Riyadh, inside the King Abdulaziz Historical Center. It lies about two kilometres north of the old city, roughly half a mile from Masmak fort.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed nearby, so use a map app to guide you. Start from the old city of Riyadh near Masmak fort; the palace is roughly half a mile away, about two kilometres north of the old city. Look for Murabba Palace or the King Abdulaziz Historical Center. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a straightforward view of the palace and its wall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and want the wall, gate and building in one frame. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as brickwork, engraved ornament and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front exterior facade, near the main gate). The two-storey mud-brick Najdi facade with its crenellated parapets, triangular windows and carved wooden doors, framed by the palace grounds. You are close to the building's northern edge, so expect to frame the palace and its surrounding wall from fairly near.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the palace's edges up with them so the walls look straight. Keep some of the wall or gate in the foreground to give a sense of scale. If you can't fit the whole building in, take a wide shot and then a few close detail shots of the texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the adobe keeps its warm colour. Try portrait mode only for people standing in front of the walls, not for the building itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the walls and is more comfortable in Riyadh's heat. Midday sun can flatten the texture and cast harsh shadows.

text.access_note: Murabba Palace is a museum within the King Abdulaziz Historical Center, so access, tickets and photography rules may apply; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer on the walls than midday sun.
Midday heat in Riyadh can make visiting uncomfortable.
From the stand-here point you are close to the northern edge of the building and may see mainly the wall and upper parts of the palace.
Photography rules inside the museum may vary and should be checked with the official site.

name: Riyadh TV Tower
label: Riyadh TV Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Riyadh TV Tower' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/5150052176: the OpenStreetMap point 'Riyadh TV Tower'.
notes: Landmark broadcasting tower on the western side of the city.

text.description:
The Riyadh TV Tower is a 170-metre television tower in the Al-Wisham neighbourhood of Riyadh. Construction began in 1975 and finished in 1982, and it was the tallest structure in Saudi Arabia until 2000, when Al-Faisaliah Tower overtook it. Its shape is simple and graphic, which suits a phone camera well: the tower rises from triangular marble entrances striped with dark bands, and those bands make strong leading lines in the front courtyard.

The phone icon on the map is in the front courtyard, near the triangular marble entrance. From here you get a close, low-angle view of the entrance with the tower climbing above it and the dark marble stripes filling the foreground. It is a quieter, more graphic picture than the wide garden view. If you would rather have that wider view, the King Abdulaziz Historical Center looks across its landscaped gardens to the tower, and it is at its best lit up against the evening sky.

The tower is part of Ministry of Information premises, so keep to public ground and stay out of any gated areas. Do not photograph security staff or restricted zones. The tower is not open for tours and photography inside is prohibited, so plan to shoot from outside only. Take a few frames at different heights, as a low angle makes the tower look taller.
text.geographic_location: The tower stands in the Al-Wisham neighbourhood of Riyadh, within Ministry of Information premises.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route to the tower, starting from the Al-Wisham area of Riyadh. The phone icon on the map is at the tower itself, in the front courtyard near the triangular marble entrance, so there is no walk from the phone icon on the map to the subject. Confirm that the courtyard is open to the public before you set out. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the entrance and the full height of the tower from close up. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less stretching at the edges. A 2x telephoto, if your phone has one, helps you pick out the marble stripes or the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The tower is right at this spot, so the photo shows the entrance and the tower above it, with the striped dark marble bands in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone low, near knee height, and tilt it up so the entrance and the tower rise together. Turn on gridlines and line up the marble stripes so they lead the eye towards the tower. For a different picture, the King Abdulaziz Historical Center offers a wider view of the lit tower over the gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch on gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the dark marble stays rich.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight suits the close courtyard view, as the marble stripes show up clearly. For the wider garden view from the King Abdulaziz Historical Center, the evening is best, when the tower is lit against the sky.

text.access_note: The tower is on Ministry of Information premises and is not open for tours, and the courtyard may be restricted, so confirm access before you go.

name: Al Thumairi Gate
label: Al Thumairi Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'طريق الملك فيصل' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'الثميري' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q120824260: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Reconstructed gate of the old city wall.

text.description: Al Thumairi Gate is a rare piece of old Riyadh that you can still walk up to. It is an earth-built fortified gateway from the 18th century, with a round mudbrick watchtower attached. It is also known as Bab al-Marwah and the al-Ahsa Gate. It once served as the main way into the walled town from the east, until 1954, and it was restored by 1992 as part of the Qasr al-Hukm District works. The gate is named after Hassan al-Thumairi, a guard killed at the Battle of Dalaqa in 1747. Al Thumairi Street, which runs east to west through the district, takes its name from the gate. The gate photographs well because of its texture and simple shapes: sand-coloured walls, the rounded tower and the dark opening of the gateway, set against the modern road in front. That contrast tells the story of the old city and the new one in a single frame. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines to line up the tower and the walls. Take one wide shot to show the setting and one closer shot of the mudbrick surface. For a different angle, walk up to the gate itself for a close view, or look along Al Thumairi Street to see the gate framing the old streets beyond.
text.geographic_location: The gate is in the ad-Dirah neighbourhood of central Riyadh, in the eastern part of the Qasr al-Hukm District, on the old city's former eastern edge. It overlooks King Faisal Street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head for the Qasr al-Hukm District in ad-Dirah, in the old centre of Riyadh. Ask to be dropped on King Faisal Street at the gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural frontal view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the road, pavement or surroundings stop you stepping back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details such as the mudbrick and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on طريق الملك فيصل (opposite the gate, on the King Faisal Street side). The gate seen from the street that it overlooks, giving a frontal view with the road in the foreground. Keep to the pavement and watch the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the gateway and use the gridlines to keep the walls and the tower upright. Include a little of the road to show the gate's place in the city, then take a closer second shot. For a different view, try the close-up of the gate itself, or Al Thumairi Street with the gate framing the old buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the sky does not wash out and the mud walls keep their colour. Panorama is not needed here; a single steady frame works best.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and warmer on the walls. Avoid the harshest midday sun, which flattens the texture.

text.access_note: Check access conditions and any photography rules at the gate and its tower on the day.

name: Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque
label: Grand Mosque
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q55614335: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Imam Turki bin Abdullah Grand Mosque, also called the Grand Mosque of Riyadh, stands in Deera Square in the ad-Dirah neighbourhood, right beside the al-Hukm Palace compound. A grand mosque has stood on this site since around 1830, in the reign of Turki bin Abdullah Al Saud. The present building dates from 1992, when it was rebuilt in the Modern Najdi style, and it reopened in January 1993. It seats 17,000 worshippers and covers 16,800 square metres, which makes it one of the largest mosques in Saudi Arabia. It won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1995.

It photographs well because of its colour and its simple, strong shapes. The outside is mostly brown Riyadh limestone, which looks golden when lit after dark. The rectangular minarets give you clean vertical lines, and two bridges link the mosque to the palace across as-Safaat Square, so you can include some of the square around it.

Start wide to show the mosque with the square in front of it. Then move in on the minaret and the stonework for a second shot. Keep a little space around the building so the walls and minaret tops are not cropped. Stay aware of worshippers and keep your phone discreet around prayer times.
text.geographic_location: In the ad-Dirah neighbourhood of Riyadh, in Deera Square next to the al-Hukm Palace compound.
text.directions_text: There are no public transport stops listed for this spot, so head to Deera Square in the ad-Dirah area, beside al-Hukm Palace. From there the mosque is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the mosque and the open square together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or barriers stop you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the minaret and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Deera Square. The mosque's facade and minarets across the open square, with the square's fountains in the foreground. From there you can see the building across the open space in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the minaret on one of the vertical lines so it stays straight. Include a strip of open square in the foreground to show the scale. Then zoom in for a tighter shot of the limestone walls and the minaret top.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sunlit stone to focus, then pull the exposure slider down a little so the limestone keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the limestone looks golden under the lights, or in the morning when the square is quieter. Try a few frames at dusk, when the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship in a public square, so dress modestly and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and prayer-time restrictions.
claims_not_in_sources: Mosques usually expect modest dress, and visits or photography inside may be limited around prayer times.
The square outside is quieter in the morning than in the evening.
A phone with a telephoto lens can zoom in on the minaret from the stand-here point, which is about 136 m away.
After dark, night mode works best if the phone is held steady against a wall or railing.

notes: Traditional market selling antiques, carpets and clothing.

text.description:
Souq al-Zal is a traditional market in the ad-Dirah area of old Riyadh, known for carpets and for agarwood (oud). Its name comes from the Gulf Arabic word for a floor rug, and rugs are still what the place is best known for. The market covers almost 9.5 acres and its origins go back to 1901, so it is one of the older markets in the city. It was renovated by 2005 and was one of the entertainment zones used during Riyadh Season in 2022.

It photographs well because of the density: narrow lanes, stalls packed with goods and people moving through. The rug displays are the obvious picture, but a quieter and more documentary shot is to turn into the narrow alleys between the stalls, where vintage items fill the frame. Stacked rugs and textiles in warm, dim light also make a good close-up.

Keep your phone ready rather than raised all the time, and be patient in the busier lanes. Ask a vendor before photographing them or their stall, and do not photograph individual people without their consent. A friendly word and a purchase, if you wish, usually make everyone more relaxed. Wipe the lens before you start, as market dust settles on it quickly.
text.geographic_location: Souq al-Zal is in the ad-Dirah neighbourhood of Riyadh, east of the al-Hukm Palace compound in the Qasr al-Hukm District.
text.directions_text: No Metro or tram stop is listed for this spot. Souq al-Zal is in ad-Dirah, east of the al-Hukm Palace compound in the Qasr al-Hukm District, so head for that area. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is at the subject itself, so there is no extra walk. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lanes and stalls; it copes best with the dim light. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only where a lane is very tight, and keep people away from the edges of the frame, where it stretches them. Use telephoto (2x-3x) for details such as rug patterns and vintage items without pointing the phone into someone's face.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see tight, atmospheric lanes packed with goods and people passing through, which shows how dense the market is.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the lane along a diagonal or the centre line, so it leads the eye into the market. Include a few stalls on each side to show how crowded it is. For a second picture, move to the carpet displays and shoot stacked rugs and textiles close up, with the warm light and the vendors' goods filling the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the lane to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour and the shadows do not turn muddy. If the phone offers night mode in dim corners, hold it steady against a wall or post while it captures. A Live Photo can catch movement in the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No single time is confirmed, so go when you can walk around calmly. Expect it to be busier at some times than others, and go when you have room to compose your shots.

text.access_note: Souq al-Zal is a traditional market and public shopping area; check the official site before you go for any access or event arrangements.
